speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview is with Hazel Corbiel, taped at Kellogg, Idaho, July 30, 1975, by Connie Bichard. We'll go ahead and talk for a minute and then. Okay, I have sort of a fact sheet that I want to fill out. We can either do this quickly if you start talking about things or we can go through this and fill it out quickly and then we can just talk. But we'll see how it goes. Okay, now you are?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hazel Corbiel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: E-L-E or E-L?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: E-I-L-L. Oh. It's French. Oh, Hazel's E-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Did you ever have a nickname Hazel? You ever said?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Really I. When I worked for the hardware store in about 39 to 40, the woman who ran it was a very fluttery lady. She was competent, very businesslike and all that, but fluttery. And she was forever saying, Hazy Bug, we need this done or that done. She had a real high school device.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hazy Bug.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Other than that, and other than working for her, she's the only person who ever gave me a nickname and I can still hear her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was your maiden name, Hazel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was a very complicated thing. My mother's family was living in Virginia, West Virginia, when she met my father. And they were married there. And later he made a trip up to Canada to visit his parents, who were on the Canadian side of Niagara Falls. And he and his dad went hunting while he was up there, and he was accidentally shot and killed. This was three months before I was born. And he had planned to return to her, but her parents at that time were just preparing to move out west again. Well, there she was, a 19-year-old bride and very pregnant. And so she came with them. In fact, my father's folks had been trying throughout that time to have the marriage broken up because they were a very aristocratic British background, although they'd been in Canada for quite some time. And my mother's family were immigrant, was an immigrant family from Norway. And they didn't, they felt this was beneath their particular family. So my mother had letters from them urging that it be broken up. So anyways, there was no chance of her going toward their home. And she started to leave with her folks. They got as far as North Dakota. And I was, they stopped long enough for me to get born there and baptized there and then moved on to Washington state. And from there, she went to Canada where she was cooking when the railroad was coming through for a railroad crew up in Saskatchewan. She met a man there and married him. Now, I was at that time, I was probably not quite two years old. But in those days, they felt that the child would have a more respectful attitude toward the man of the house if she thought it to be her father. So I was never known by my rightful name of Hazel Brewery.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was only later that you found out?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I was, well, just before they had me married, why I...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before you got married yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it was just before I was married that they told me, that my mother told me. Frankly, it's a subject that comes up frequently in the paper. Should a child be told? And I would say that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you feel about that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To me, it was the greatest relief ever because my stepdad was an awful man.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, so then you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I had a younger sister, seven years, almost seven years younger. And as a child, I often wondered why in the world he couldn't like me at all. He was always so outrageously mean and the partiality went so far that it was... It was always... I mean, I was scared to death of him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you never understood why?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I never understood why. No? It didn't hurt. In fact, it was nothing but relief when I found out that he was not my father.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't that something?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So I often wonder when I see these items in the papers and magazines about whether or not a child should be told. And I know in my case, I could have had a far better understanding because even as a child, I had more understanding than many adults did. And so it was nothing but relief. However, I had gone... Well, all the years that I had in any public schooling was under the name of Weisenberg and under the attitude of thinking that he was my father.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he ever adopt you legally?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, no, no, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So really, your name was Drury all that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, Drury, D-R-E-W-E-R-Y. However, so many of my legal papers and everything were in the other name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, well, why don't I put both names down?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: His name was Weisenberg, W-E-I-S-E-N-B-E-R-G. And then they pretty much arranged a marriage for me when I was 16 because that was the only logical disposition of a 16-year-old girl. I mean, I wanted education so badly that I cried for days. He was young, that is, he was only five years older than I. But we had absolutely nothing in common then, or did we, at any time. The marriage lasted for 17 years because I had been brought up to think that you make a contract, that's that. But so that name was Pears, P-E-A-I-R-S.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, so you, and then Pears, how, what is it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: P-E-A-I-R-S. I guess it's of Welsh origin. And then I...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was your date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, December 4th, 1909.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Carrington, North Dakota. C-A-R-R-I-N-G-T-O-U.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. And then your first residence in Idaho was where? Did you come with your husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. My... I said I was married at 16. I had gone to 24 schools before that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let me ask you a couple of questions about that early marriage. Were most girls at the time getting married young like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Most of them, no, I won't say most of them, no. Many of them were getting married early, but it was usually because of pregnancy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And when, and this was funny because...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Way back then? I thought that the stigma against that was so...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, the stigma was there, but you had seven-month babies in those days.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean they were born premature? No, they were...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the explanation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that just shocks me. I didn't know about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, so many, especially a lot of older people, will sit around quite smugly and talk about the regenerate group that we have now. But really, except for the cover-ups, there was more hypocrisy there. But now, in my situation, the wedding date was set for two weeks after my birthday. It was my birthday, 4th of December. I was married on the 16th of December. And when I went into the principal's office, I told him that I would be quitting. And it was all I could do to keep from crying because I loved school wherever I went. That was the one delight in my life. But immediately he looked me over at the right places. He says, you too? And I was quite taken aback. I wasn't really. I was very innocent. And didn't quite know what it was all about. And then I found out later that he had made a comment aside. There was one of the girls that I'd been quite friendly with had heard him make the comment on the side that he didn't know what they were going to do. That was the third this month they'd quit school because they were pregnant.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh my gosh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But the heartache of getting married that early in those days was that schooling was done. It was finished. But I found out later on that I had lots of time, but there was no books. Whenever I'd been in school, at least I had access to books. And I'd been a reader from the time that I first started in first grade. And there were no books, no papers, no anything in the home I was in. And so I went back to see if possibly I could enroll again and finish high school. But it wouldn't be the proper atmosphere for the innocent. And this definitely, it's only been in the last, well, I guess since war years, that it's been acceptable for a married person to continue on in school, which is wonderful. On the other hand, I do think that there should be a few restrictions. I mean, if a boy gets married at 16 or 17, I don't think that he should be encouraged to take part in all the other things. Voices sure come through different, don't they?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does it sound different to you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, who knows? I know my voice is deep. I mean, I just... It's clear.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did they choose the man that you were going to marry? Did you know him before?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we lived in Preston, B.C. for a while, two, three different places. But the last place we were in in Preston, B.C. was a small town restaurant.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was your father working in a restaurant?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My folks operated this. They did a little bit of everything. And they operated this small cafe, and there were three rooms upstairs that they could rent out. And a family had come in from the Prairie States and bought a saloon that was just across the alley from this restaurant, but they couldn't move into it immediately, and they stayed in these rooms. I was nine years old at that time. Well, they were a family that was quite similar to my family, moving from one place to the other forever. I mean, every year or two, moving. Our two families became acquainted there. Then, later on, we moved to Iowa and several places in Iowa, then came back to Idaho, eventually moved to Mullin, Idaho, and that family that had been up there was living in Mullin.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The same one? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Later on, we moved from Mullin to Hayden Lake, and eventually from Hayden Lake to Kellogg. When we came to Kellogg, this family was living here. So you see, there had been an association. There hadn't been letter correspondence or anything. And this was the last time I was nine years old there. I was 15 when I came to Kellogg. But their oldest son was 21. He had a job in the mines. He was a very big man because he could flex his muscles and have a job. He actually supported his folks. His folks lived with us during the 17 years of the...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All 17 years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There are things I'd like to say that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Go ahead. I'd like to have you say anything that you want to say.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I hate to hurt anyone, but... You have a very ambitious, very self-centered mother-in-law.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Makes life pretty difficult.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And an acquiescent attitude. It doesn't really build for any kind of marriage, no matter how seriously one takes the contract.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Speaking of marriages in those days... They talk about many marriages now are kind of hit and miss and peculiar and so on and so forth. There I was, just past my 16th birthday. My mother went along with me to... As the saying was then, stand up for me. No other witness came along. We drove to Wallace, got the marriage license at the courthouse, went to a Justice of the Peace to be married. He looked at me and looked at my mother and said, how old is she? And she said, she's 16. He said, do you give your consent? She said, yes. And I never was questioned as to a yes, no, or go to the devil.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No one asked you if you wanted this or not? No. No. Your wishes were not considered?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It just wasn't necessary. I mean, I imagine that the judge had the same attitude that the school principal had had. That it would be... It was two years before my first child was born. But it was just taken for granted. That anyone who got married at that age, well, that must be it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you feel like your parents wanted to get rid of you? Is that why they wanted you to get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Well, I didn't know it at the time, but my mother's health was very bad. Was beginning, becoming very bad. She died two years later. And her marriage had not been happy. She wasn't the kind to complain. There again, she had married this man. And so, that's the way you make it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was her marriage...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You must lie. That was a thing of those days.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You accepted it. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But on the other hand, she knew the man well enough that I think that perhaps the one dread that she may have had about... There was very... There really was no communication between us. But I think that the real fear she had that she might die was what would become of me if I were left to him. It was safer to have me safely married to someone, you see? It wasn't a matter of richness. Yes, he had a job that made him steady. But it was a matter of not only inviting him to the house constantly, but we went to church in a group. And that is my mother. Stepdad was the owner. Of course, he would have been glad to get rid of one more to feed at any time. Not that there was any big family, but he just... I think he begrudged me from the time...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You didn't have a very happy childhood then, did you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. There was no childhood. One thing that my mother's family all believed in was that work was to be done. And from the time I can remember, there was work. In fact, now it's almost 66. It's the first time in my life that I have felt my time is my own, to do with it as I want. I work if I feel like it, and I read if I feel like it. And no responsibility to anyone. And I find it a very happy start of a living.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I guess you deserve it, after all those years of work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother came from a family that was do-it-yourselfers, and they also believed that to keep hands busy was the best solution to everything. And I can remember out in the homestead in Canada, long before I was of school age, piecing quilts by hand, and if one little backstitch... If you know what a backstitch is, one little backstitch was out of place. And we're along that old seam, and I'd have to pick the stitches out with a needle, go back there and start over and do it over. By the time we moved into Swift Current, where I started school, and that was the fall before I was seven years old, there's another thing. In all the years that I did go to school, I... only once, I believe, did I start school when school started. And only once or twice was I going to school when the school was over, in the spring. There'd be changes in schools in between. But what I mean is, the folks would always seem to move a little too late to get me started in the beginning of the semester, or period, or whatever it was called at the time. And they would always move someplace else just before school was out, a month or six weeks or two months before school was out. And so it was with my first year in school. But even at that time, my mother took in sewing, and I'd better be home right on time to start making buttonholes and do the hand-stitching and hems. And I was seven years old then. I didn't feel put upon because of the work. But now, reading was considered a waste of time. And as I developed such an awful yin for reading, and I exhausted libraries in every school I went to. I read Last Miserables when I was in the fifth grade, both great big, thick volumes of it. And everything that was readable in any school I went to. But I couldn't read it at home. Maybe that made a better student of me, because I had to come home with good grades. So I would rush through my lessons and then rush through the library books. But there was always work to be done at home. Always. Not always the same thing. There wasn't sewing. I lived in Bonners Ferry, Idaho. The first summer we were there, the folks had a... They moved on to an old deserted farm. It was out on the south bench, as it was called then. And it was quite... There were quite large old farm acreages up there, many of them deserted. This one, someone had started to build a house on it, but never finished. It wasn't finished inside at all. It was just the outside board and sort of a roof on it. But somehow my dad got permission to farm, to live there and farm that for the summer on a share crop basis or something. He had to put in so many acres of potatoes. Well, we had three cows. And they would turn the cows' booths to graze down by the railroad tracks. They would really drop off from this bench. Oh, I don't know. It might have been 30 feet or so right down to where the railroad tracks were in the lower level of the ground. And there was good grazing along there. But at the time of the day when the trains would be coming through, and freights were not always right on time, you know, I'd have to go down there and keep an eye on those cows to make certain that they weren't going to be on the track when the train came. But that wasn't to be wasted time. In those days, women wore camisoles over their corsets. This camisole was cut straight around at the top and had straps over it. But it was quite a thing to have a wide lace band, a crocheted lace band. The ones that I made were probably about four inches wide. There were many different types of stitches.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any left? Do you have any patterns?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Definitely not. But in the course of that summer, I crocheted these bands for other people at $3 each. I was 12 years old that summer. And I don't know how many of those I crocheted. And they were supposed to be... I was supposed to have money to have some real nice school clothes. And I know that was my mother's intent because I was not only always a stranger in school. I was always horribly, disastrously dressed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because you were poor?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and even if there was money, it shouldn't be wasted. And then, of course, there was my stepfather's attitude. However, my mother's attitude, too, was that clothes were just a matter of vanity. She was a good seamstress. She made beautiful things for customers. But I can't remember ever having a garment at home that fit me because she always allowed for extra growth and shrinkage. Most of them were worn out before they ever fit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before they ever fit. You could grow into them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. And there again, the economy of it. They were always made much longer than anybody else's, and then hemmed sometimes like that. Of course, I know I grew because she was very small herself, and I guess she thought there was going to be no end to where I went. I was always the tallest girl in the class, and I don't feel that tall now because the new generation of girls are tall. But it was really quite a handicap in those years. Well, anyway, I don't know how many of those I crocheted. I know there were many, many of them. And most of the crocheting was done down there herding the cows. And we'd have orders for maybe three or four from one customer, see. So there was no worry about that. But when the time came to get those school clothes, my stepdad insisted that he should go with me, and he was going to get me a pair of shoes that by God were going to last me. In those days, men's and boys' work shoes were made extremely wide with a great big humped-up hard toe. Have you ever seen any of those in museums or anything? It was quite commonplace.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he made you buy those for yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's what he got for me. The shoe came down with a great big built-up toe like that. And this was really, I mean, it was humped up. And boys, oh, say, seventh and eighth grades and so forth, they could kick everything with that, and they were very apt to say all right. They came up about seven inches. Now there's a size difference. I had quite large feet. If he got some that were too short for me, goodness knows there was plenty of room in there for my feet to spread out this way. They were a dollar cheaper than if you got the next size. So they were not only the most ungainly things ever put on a girl, but they were also entirely too short. And to this day, the only part of my body that has occasioned any distress for me is my feet. And that was just one. In Swift Current, Saskatchewan, there was a secondhand store there. He had some old ladies' button shoes. I know you've seen those in the gay nineties. High French heel. It was a little bit of a curved heel. And then they came up, and they had a row of buttons down here. And were extremely pointed. Well, here I was, a child nine years old with rather chubby feet. They got four pairs of those at 50 cents a pair, cut off the heel, so it brought it down. The things were, they were small size in the beginning, and they were so tight, the first pair, I just hurt. I walked over a mile to school in those every day for the first several months that we were there. And eventually, toward the last of it, there'd be holes cut in the side to make room for my feet.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the other children...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There was just this half-sister of mine, when I...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your schoolmates make fun of you with these kinds of things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Don't they ever. Besides that, I was a stranger. Perhaps that did me a lot of good, because what I mean is, in later life...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You knew how to...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I could always understand the other person's problems or distresses. There are times, of course, that one doesn't need to be too concerned about people's problems, because much of it is of their own doing. However, there can be so much hurt through ignorance. And I guess that's what it is. Because... My stepdad was extremely penny-pinching. My mother was, too. However, I do think that had she had any realization that such things could have a lifetime effect on a person's health situation... I've been lucky. I've managed to put up with it. But had she thought of it in those terms, she would have managed somehow. She would have gotten something from the standpoint of health. She wouldn't for vanity, but she would for health. But it was a matter of ignorance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I have some more things to fill in.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But life wasn't all hard, either. You say an unhappy childhood. I shouldn't have gotten started on that, because I don't really think of it... The childhood is so far, far back. The first marriage is so far back. Every phase of my life has been a different life. I've had some very good, very wonderful years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, we'll get to those. Let's see. Your original locale before you came to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Iowa was before that, and British Columbia before that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember what year you came to Bonner's Ferry, approximately?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 21, I think it was. No, it was either 20 or 21. It was just before Thanksgiving, a week before Thanksgiving.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how did you come?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That is a story.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I mean, what kind of transportation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh, that's what I mean. We'd been in Iowa. My dad had had some work that summer. My mother had taken in some sewing. But they had left British Columbia to go to Iowa in the first place. He had relatives there, and they'd been there for the intent to just go for a visit, and they stayed for about two years. But they were anxious to get back out west, because they had left a few belongings they had stored in British Columbia. So they'd been skimping and saving to get money enough to get some kind of transportation out here. We'd gone to Iowa by train. Found an old Detroiter car body in the junk, at the city dump for junk, city junk piles, they called it, in Algona, Iowa. And somehow he managed to scrounge an old Ford chassis. He set the Detroiter body on top of the Ford chassis. Now that was the Ford Model T, and that was a little bit of a chassis, and the hood was a little bit of a short thing. The Detroiter was about twice as high as the hood should be. This was just boarded up in front all black. And then this body stuck way out beyond the Ford chassis. A very peculiar arrangement. That was before the car bodies were closed in. There were curtains with little ice and glass windows in them that you buttoned on if the weather was bad.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's how you came?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Everything they owned was in that. Had the old spoke wheels, wooden spoke wheels, and thin little tires around them. And everything they owned was in that. Well, they'd had $700 and some dollars saved up to come out west with. And on the night before we left, my stepdad had gone out, I guess, to celebrate by a drink or two, although he wasn't... He would drink at unpredictable times. He wasn't what one could call really a drunkard. But he had been engaged in conversation with some slicker that took his $700 of his $750 in return for some kind of sticks of solder that he was supposed to sell for a big profit. And he was going to make all this profit all the way out. Well, it really wasn't that profitable, and it did leave them without any money to start with except that $50. And when I said they had everything they owned on this car, what they couldn't put inside, they tied on top. And the things that they tied on in back, around fenders, included a wash tub and a copper-bottom boiler and a couple of extra tires and a bundle of spokes that he resurrected from the damp that would fit these things. Well, then every day would be a real hard day's journey. It was the rare tourist that ever made 100 miles in a day in those days. Now this sounds strange when you think of how quickly you can go over what used to be the Yellowstone Trail through Montana and into the Dakotas. In those days, they were just building some of those roads, knocking them out of gumbo. And besides the cars, if you did 35 miles an hour, you were speeding. I mean, perhaps. So it was a slow process. And by the end of any day's journey, the first thing to do was to stop someplace where you could have access to water and fill the tubs in the boiler or whatever with water, take all those tires, those wheels off the car, remove the tires, put the wheels to soak in these tubs of water.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why did they soak?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the friction of all this driving, the air friction, the heat friction, and the juggling and jostling would dry out the wood to the extent that the spokes would have to start falling out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So this was a nightly occurrence to put the wheels to soak. And sometimes the spokes in the wheels would become so worn that when they'd replace them after a thorough soaking, they would have pieces of canvas they'd tuck over the end and then pound them into place. This went on. It took us two months to come from Iowa out here because they had to stop and work once in a while. And the cities that people really aimed for, I mean the overnight stops, the people really aimed for, were the places that tourists coming the other direction would tell you they had a tourist park. A tourist park was in a place where there might be a few trees, there might be some limbs broken down, or some of them there might be a merchant right close around like a little country grocery store that would encourage the tourists to park there by having a load of wood unloaded every day so that you could build your campfire. It was out in the open. You could pitch your tents if you wanted to or sleep on the ground if you wanted to. There were no cabins or anything like that. But those tourist parks were such a godsend to the travelers. A great many of them were like my family, my family were traveling to go someplace specifically, moving, and had their stuff with them. Nobody but nobody ever crossed that from Iowa to the West had a car that looked like ours. This was beyond belief. I've wished so many times that I had a picture of that Detroiter body sitting on top of the little old Model T chassis.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How old were you then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was, I suppose, well, it would make me around 10 1⁄2, going on 11.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You seem to remember it pretty clearly.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a good recall. Way back. That reminds me of this friend of mine, Ruby L. Holt, who has written books. She so often, in some of her historical stuff, will send her work to me for critical reading, and time and again I have questioned her description of some of it. Well, one time she had an article about a lumberjack back in the 1920s going to work in the woods, that he packed his lunch bucket and his thermos, and immediately I wrote back and said, Ruby, they didn't have thermoses then. They had the old inn bucket with an inn set at the top, and they'd have the coffee in the bottom half, and the inn set at the top would have their lunch, whatever it would be. It might even be baked beans or something like that. But the lower part was hung over a little bit of a campfire to heat that coffee, and if they had an upper lunch that needed heating, it could heat there. If not, they took out that part, the sandwich and that sort of thing. And she says, my gosh, she'd been washing that kind of lunch buckets from the time she was a kid, and yet found herself writing about thermos, because she's become adjusted to it. But I do have a natural recall.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hazel, who went with you then? Who came from Iowa to Bonner's Ferry?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother and my stepdad and my little sister.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that—do you just have one sister? Yes. Okay. Now I want to get quickly your mother's maiden name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lily Hong, H-O-N-G. That sounds Oriental, but she was Norwegian.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did she have—you mentioned she was a seamstress. Did she have other ways of bringing in income? Did she have jobs and anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Yes, she—in fact, she worked all the time, no matter where we were. Can you remember the major— In Bonner's Ferry, when we were out on that farm on the south bench where I said I was— that was just for the summer season where I would take care of the cows and go shade things. One of the farmers some distance from there had several sheep. She went to them and arranged to cut the wool from the sheep before butchering season. And she carded the wool and prepared quilt bats with cheesecloth covering for that woman in return for keeping half of the wool.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean—does that mean she made it into yarn?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Carding—have you ever seen wool cards?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There are a couple of flat things about the size of this with nails sticking out on each side. And you have them with the nails facing. You lay a piece of wool in, you pull it like this, and that separates the fibers of the wool. And all the weeds and seeds and things, a good portion of them fall out. After you've worked them that way, so you've got the large weeds and stuff done out of it, then you wash the stuff good, you dry it in the sun, then you start the carding process all over because you've lost some more junk out of it. I've carded wool, too. Because she was—even though I was born in 1909, which by all rules and regulations should be partially civilized time to be born, my mother was a pioneering staff that went back beyond that. And so I was introduced to things of that type that were not commonplace in 1909. I mean, or in the growing years following 1909, you see. But anyway, she carded enough wool batts for the neighbors that we had all the wool batts we needed for years to come, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then after that is when you made it into a yarn?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, after that. It has to be thoroughly carded before it can be spun into yarn. But for quilt batts, when you finally have carded out all this muck and mess out of it, you have a narrow piece of wool filler that looks very much like a polyester filler. And these narrow pieces, when they're put on, there'd be cheesecloth backing stretched on a quilt frame. All right, then these pieces are laid overlapping, just about half overlapping like that, in rows in there. And the next row is half overlapping both directions, see? Then the other piece of cheesecloth is put over the top, and these are tied together and stitched together. And that makes a quilt batt like a polyester quilt batt, but it's pure wool.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Pure wool. I guess you don't have those anymore.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't wash them very often, either.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's true, too. When was she born? What was her birth date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1889, January 10th. She died before she was 39 years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh. And where was she born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Brainerd, Minnesota. I said she was a foreign extraction definitely, but she was born in Brainerd. I mean, in Little Norway or whatever.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was the date of her death, then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: November... Geez, I think it was November 16th. It was 1928, anyway.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's just the year that's important.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was in November that I...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember what year she was married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She married my father in 1908, and she married Wiesenberg in 1912.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Now, do you know anything about your father's family, then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you find out later?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Before my marriage, my mother not only told me about the first marriage, but had a bundle of letters that she had saved until then, including marriage certificate, including letters from his mother trying to get the marriage annulled. She didn't want her friends in Canada to know that he had married what she called a servant girl, and this was how it was referred to all the way through. And there were also very kindly letters from his father. His father, I think, must have been a very fine person. But his grandfather was the engineer who planned the first power plant at Niagara Falls. And apparently was a very well-educated and very competent and creative engineer, construction engineer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, what was your father's first name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: William Henry... I started to say, though, after she told me all this, she suggested that she and I both write to Niagara Falls and the Canadian... Yes, Niagara Falls on the Canadian side, too. It's Ontario. To try to get in touch with some of my father's family because she thought that I should establish some connections with them. And she wrote a letter and then had me write one and enclosed it with it and sent them both to the postmaster there with a note asking if they could get in touch with anyone in this family. His mother was still living at that time. That was in 1926. And I received a letter in return. Well, my mother received what one would say was a note. Thank you for getting in touch. I received a letter that was so probably a page of the TABA paper like they used to use for writing letters. And in it she said that it was very strange to be brought to her attention because she'd never known whether I was ever born or existed or anything else. And that if I wished to communicate with her, that it would be fine. She would try to reply to any letters she received. But she did not like the letters to be sent to that address. Instead, she had a trusted friend that I should post them to her because after all, her present family, she had remarried after her husband had died. And her present family knew nothing of the earlier association between her son and my mother. Under the circumstances, I never wrote to her. I never cried even in those days. And I've had no contact with them. As I said, my father was killed in a hunting accident. He had three brothers. I know that he was extremely fond of all three. My mother had letters that had been written to her congratulating her husband on their marriage and raving about pictures of her and very felicitous letters in every way. But all three of those brothers were killed or died from injuries in World War I.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh. Did your father have an occupation or a job?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He had been sent to, I believe it was West Point. I don't have any picture. My mother had all these letters and things. And after her death, which wasn't too long afterwards, my stepfather just burned everything with a little mercy. And I was too young to question or grab. There were so many things that were burned. But the picture was in the uniform of a military school. And there was so much told me at that one time. But my mother was so disturbed. And ours had been a noncommunicating family. And there were so many questions I would like to have asked. But I didn't want to create all this disturbance. And so they were never answered. But I believe it was some kind of an agreement between Canada and West Point. There was some kind of an exchange system there that he was entered in the West Point. You see, West Point wasn't too far from the Williamsburg area where they lived. So he was employed in his own right at the time he married her. I gathered not. He was of age. But I gathered that he perhaps was not employed, but that his parents were really supporting him in this school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see. And he was quite young when he died then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. He couldn't have been more than 22 at the most, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know the year of his birth or place?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, no, no. Because that would all have been, as I say, there was only one session with my mother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you don't know the date of his death and either the year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, except that it was, yes, I do. It was three months before I was born.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that would have been?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In 1909. It would have been the long of September, I suppose, of 1909.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. And then you had one sister?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Half-sister.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was her name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Generva. That's G-E-N-E-R-V-A.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. No brothers. Now, let's see. I have a section here on spouse and children. I guess we'll... You had two marriages, right? Well, let's...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have two children by the first marriage. In fact, there were three born to me in that marriage. They were all born at home. The doctor came to the house, to the first one. As I say, the mother-in-law lived there, my both in-laws.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I might check this.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She, of course, knew all about childbirth, but she had never and was not about to ever be participating in a birth. Well, that was all right. I didn't want her participating in the actual birth. I wanted my children to at least have a little security in their beginning. I was very strong, very healthy. There were three roomers at the house, and I'd been doing all the washing by hand for them, hanging it up and all the rest of it, and the cooking and dishwashing and what have you. As I said, I had a strong back. So I was in extremely good health. But when it was evident that I was going to be giving birth on that particular day, there were various things that had to be done first and so on and so forth. And finally, when the pains became fairly regular, well, I did go to bed. And I had not lain down very long until I felt absolutely certain that the child was being born and kept telling my husband, who was there, to go for the doctor. We were over a mile out of town. And I was afraid the doctor might be busy. Anyway, I thought he should be there. My mother-in-law said, Don't you bother the doctor now. She hasn't shed a tear yet, and she's going to do some hollering before this is over. And he positively was not. He was used to doing what his mother said. And she knew. She'd had children. She knew. And I was becoming absolutely panicked, not because of any extreme internal distress, but the emotional distress of knowing that this child was being born. And this was about 4.30 in the afternoon, and two of the roomers came home from work and heard me absolutely yelling to get the doctor. The baby is coming. And heard my mother-in-law yelling back, Now you just stopped that. Now you're going to have to work harder than that because they don't come that easy. You're going to be doing some hollering before that child comes. Well, one of these roomers took it upon himself to dash downtown and get the doctor. And the doctor was there about 20 minutes after the baby was born. And because of my strength, I had torn myself wide open, so he had to give me a shot of chloroform and sew me up. And it was no great handicap. Incidentally, the washing, the doctor insisted I stay in bed for 10 days. That was the rule in those days. Mother-in-law agreed to that. I stayed in bed for 10 days. But the washing was piled up waiting for me on the 10th day.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, gosh. What were your children's names then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Roy Stanley Pierce. And Richard Dean Pierce.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And their dates of birth? Just the years, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Roy was April 14, 1928, and Richard was February 8, 1930.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where were they born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Kellogg or out of Kellogg.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do they have an occupation now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Roy is with the Oregon State School of Forestry, and he has been ever since he got out of the Korean War. After I started out on my own, shall we say, broke loose from the bondage of mother-in-law, I managed to help Roy through college, and he's a technical forester. And immediately after college, he served his stint in the Korean War. He was in the last eight months of it. And when he came home, he immediately sent out applications for work in forestry and got on with the Oregon State School of Forestry, and he's a technical forester and has been with them ever since. He actually was working as a forest analyst until the Nixon administration, when they cut down the funds for that, so he's doing the forest analyst work on technical pay, shall we say.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I see. And what does the other son do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The other son, on his 18th birthday, enlisted in the Air Force. And, see, that was in 1948. And I thought he was going to stay in it just for one stint, but he stayed with it for 20 years, and now he's a meat cutter with one of the out-of-state markets in Salem. Roy, incidentally, is at State in Oregon, which is just out of Salem.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Did you have children by the other marriage or not?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Twenty years after Richard was born. I have a son, David, Corbill, and that is quite an experience, one of my babies, for sure.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that 1950?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he was born here in Kellogg?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I said 1947, 1949. He was born in June. It was almost 20 years after Dick.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Here in Kellogg?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. In the hospital. Cut off to a right start, after a fashion.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does he do something now, too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, he teaches at Coast Falls.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He's a teacher.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's busy all the time. He has a wonderful little wife and a new granddaughter for me. She's 10 months old now, but I have a great-grandchild who was born in January and a great-grandchild born in July.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You have a great-grandmother already. That's nice.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There was no rush in. I was 18 when my oldest was born, so that was older than a lot of girls were then. And their daughters... One of my granddaughters was born the same year that my youngest son was born.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That happened with my mother. Did it, really? She had a daughter who was like one or two when my sister had a son, so it was funny because... Isn't it funny having two little ones and ones in a hand?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I never knew. To me, I wasn't too conscious of it because my only grandchildren from those sons is all from the one son, from Richard. He was in the Air Force. He married an English girl. And staying in the Air Force for 20 years, and 17 of them spent overseas, and I was busy by that time running my own business here in town, a very demanding business. It didn't give me travel time, I'll tell you. And with the new baby here, I never saw those children. Whenever there was a reenlistment period come up, they always arranged to be with me for... It might be a week, it might be two weeks.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They came back to visit you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, but it was just a visit en route from one base to another. And it was very infrequent. And even during those visits, the shop still took my time. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, now I have a section here on personal information for you. And we've talked about a lot of the things, like your education. You said you went through school up to the age of 16 in about 24 different schools, right? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I had some wonderful, wonderful school teachers. I was always an honor student. There's a funny thing. In those days, I suppose they still exempt you from certain examinations if your grades are high enough. It seems to me I heard Dave talking about it a time or two. But it was quite commonplace then, it was a special reward to anyone who had high grades from, oh, about the seventh grade up, that you didn't have to take the examination at the end of the semester or the period, as they sometimes called it then. Well, it was my hard luck to always be exempted from it at one school, but when I'd enroll in the other, regardless of what time of the year I enrolled, I'd have to take a major examination because they didn't believe these straight As or straight Es or straight whatever it was. And Kellogg was the worst of the lot, the superintendent, the same one that would look down his nose at me. I had straight As for excellent and a note from the teacher written on the final transfer and all the rest of it that was very high in praises of my work, my ability, and so forth. So I turned this in to the superintendent, and he snuffs it, well, country schools have a different standard than we do. We will have to absolutely, we must, have you take a thorough examination here before we know for sure how we can place you in our grade. But I still came through. They all started in this valley. They had a spelling match every Saturday, spelling bee, that was sponsored by Dr. Collins, Puroles Dentist in Spokane. The first prize was a $25 certificate. I listened to one or two of them on the radio and decided I could spell good enough for that because really during all those years of that marriage, the only reading material I had that was really my own that I could be sure of having was the dictionary.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, a dictionary.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And there was a Bible too. And I read both of them backwards and forwards and made games of the dictionary and the value. And when I heard the words that people missed on those spelling contests, I decided I could spell. But oh man, did my mother-in-law ever berate me when she thought that I was going to take part in one of those spelling contests on the air? She would make her the laughingstock of all her friends and everything else. It was absolutely ridiculous. I was not educated. I should not try it. But I tried it anyway, and I won the first Saturday. I was down there bright and shining the next Saturday, and I won that. I won the third Saturday. I won the fourth Saturday, and that time they told me this is it. They made a new ruling just as of then that we could not enter after three wins. But I won four times in a row.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I bet that made you feel good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, perhaps if she hadn't been. And she also berated me every time that I reentered because it was nothing but luck the first time. But it made me all the more determined, and I'll grant you, that I did a little studying up between times, refreshing myself. But it was... So you see, part of the education was having that dictionary when there was nothing else to read.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, let's talk about the different jobs you picked. Can you tell me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The first job I had was to take the census in 1940. Well, in taking the census, I signed up for two precincts at Warner and did a great job on them, I guess, because I could talk. I mean, there again, I could identify. There were mostly poorer families up there. They were very fine families, the majority of them. But they were... It wasn't the best residential area. And I could identify with them because I'd lived in so many different areas of the country, of the continent. And I met people from many different nationalities. And a little of that rubs off all through. I do have a good memory. And a little of the association rubs off and probably helped prepare me to meet people. And my success up there was phenomenal, really. There was no one omitted. And then the enumerator asked me to complete a couple of precincts that someone had started and had decided they just couldn't catch anybody at home or couldn't get the answers to their questions. They just barely started their precincts. They were down on Park Avenue and McKinley Avenue. So I did those. Then he asked me to take a precinct that was over in the Callaghan Division Street area that someone had only half completed there. I finished that. Finally ended up, after doing dabs here, there, and the other place, including a dab out at Pinehurst. It was Pine Creek then. There was no town. He asked me to do the mop-up work. That was a coupon in the paper asking anyone who had been missed in the census to fill in the coupon and mail it either to me or to the paper. And I would go around and get their name. The result was that I was named the outstanding enumerator in the state of Idaho. And Compton I. White was a congressman from this district at that time. Came up to this ramshackle house where I lived. I didn't own a bathrobe. I'd had a cold and slept in that day. And I had my husband's bathrobe on. He'd go to the door. He came in. Did you ever see Compton White or ever see a picture of him, the old Compton White?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I don't think so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He must have been about 6'4 or 5'0 and about yea broad. He had the broadest shoulders of anybody I ever saw. He just filled the door. And a big booming voice. The minute I opened the door, me with this old flannel bathrobe with my husband's tied around me. He reaches out, Let me shake hands with the best god damn census taker in the state of Idaho. I'll never forget that. But anyway, I had to write a human interest report on that, which is supposed to be in the files of Congress. I don't know. There was a lot to tell.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hazel, do you know what time it is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, 5 to 11.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, I have a few more minutes, but not a long time because we have to be out of our motel room by noon and I have to walk back over there. What are the other major jobs that you had then after that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, then I was also involved in politics along the way. I was the first woman from this county, this minor men's county, to run for a legislative office in politics. Actually, my census-taking work probably had little bearing on becoming acquainted with people because I made friends in that, even though I was only in the house for a few minutes. There was a feeling of friendship. I didn't realize it so much at the time being, but later on it came to life. And then, it's an entirely different story, though. I was the first woman to ever run for legislative office in this county and was so nearly successful that I ran for the first office, which was state representative, and the second office was state senator. And again, I was successful in the primaries and made a good showing in the other. But in the meantime, before the finals in the Senate race, before the finals in the Senate race, I had bought a little flower shop, but in between time I was also working at a hardware store. And I met a lot of people there and many of those became my friends.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you a clerk in the hardware store?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I was supposed to handle the kitchen department and the kitchenware, as I should say. And there were some vases and dishes, knick-knacks and things of that type. But this was during war years. In fact, I was working there when the war broke out on December 7, 1941. And they were short-handed and people were having to do a lot more of their own work. And before long I was cutting glass and setting saws and you name it. I knew more about tools than the so-called carpenters that came in wanting a hammer. You could sell them a ball-peen. You know what a ball-peen hammer is? One of those that has a knob on one end and a little bit of a thing at the other. They usually use it for tax or something. When they came in to go to work in the mines, they were supposed to have their own hammer and saw. They'd buy a ball-peen hammer and a rip saw or even a keyhole saw or anything else and turn out for work with a ball-peen hammer and that. You couldn't get the hardware merchandise, see? So when you got down to just the dregs of it, they would buy anything. Now a rip saw is when you're ripping lengthwise. Now the crosscut saw will cut across a board well. But to use one in the place of the other doesn't work well. You see, the hardware merchandising is still with me. Well, it was in 1943 that I bought the flower shop. And that was a tremendous undertaking. I mean, I went in debt for $3,000 on it, but there again it was a matter of the friends that I had made. Some of the best customers at the hardware store were people who insisted on my waiting on them all the time. And they owned several rental properties. And I would tell them about new things that were economical. They watched to pennies. But if there was something new that seemed to make sense from speeding up the painting in the house or something like that when they were reconditioning these properties, they would listen to me and sometimes try a sample of it and so on and so forth. They learned to depend upon me to be absolutely honest in my recommendations of whether I knew anything or just thought I knew it. And when the opportunity came to buy that flower shop, actually there again it was an accident. The people that owned it were friends of my boss, this woman that called me Hazy Bug. They came in trying to sell her the shop, the business. And she said, well, what in the world would I want to do with that? I've already got more work than I can do here. And they said, well, Hazel does such a good job with your artificial flowers and everything that she would be artistic in arranging flowers. She could learn it easy. You could put her in charge of it. And she said, well, I don't want to expand now. And after they left the store, she said, you know, Hazy Bug, that wouldn't be a bad idea. You could be put in charge of that and it might work out all right. You know, when I worked for her, I was paid $1.50 for a six-hour day. I walked about a mile and a quarter from home downtown, walked back up the mile and a quarter afterwards, and was paid $1.50 for a six-hour day. I had learned a great deal from her. In fact, everything that I knew about business management, I had learned by observing what she did and how she did it. But I'd never had a raise. There were times that she'd be gone two or three weeks at the time for various reasons. When she was gone, I did the posting, one time sent out the statements. But I also did all these other little things, see? Window dressing, she'd taken great pride in her window dressing. No one in town had windows like she had. When she was gone one time, after she came back, a man who was an itinerant, well, not itinerant, a man who made his living taking pictures of people and then of things in town and then selling it to the owner, came around to sell her a group of pictures she had taken of the window. And it was the window I had put in while she was gone. From then on, I was the official window dresser. But as I thought about this, I was busy working, but as I thought about it, I thought, well, if anyone as careful with their money as she is could even think, just for a minute, buying that shop and put me in to run it, why shouldn't I be able to gamble on it myself? I knew nothing about floristry, absolutely nothing. But I went to the people during my break and asked them how much they wanted for it. That was the only thing I was interested in. They wanted $3,000 for it. I had a bank account of $79. And I was really proud of that because I never had that much until I started working out. But they said, oh, maybe you can borrow something. And they said you couldn't borrow from the bank because you wouldn't have the, what's the word, security for it. But there are individuals that lend money. And one of the names that they named for me was this old couple that used to be my good, such good customers at the hardware store. So I went to them before I ever went home that evening after I got off work. And they asked me if I knew anything about the business. I said, no, but I can learn anything. I'll work hard at it. Well, they knew I was a good worker. They knew that I had a certain amount of logic on my side. And they knew as nearly as they could tell that I was honest in every respect. And, you know, they wanted me to learn. You might say it's face value because that was always true. And they checked up on me frequently to see if I was saving the money all right. And I was. I didn't have to make a payment for a year. But I was depositing money in an account to make that payment plus interest. And they were very happy with the arrangement. I was too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you owned that for?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 30 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 30 years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But Mother Hegbot was really a ranch owner.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Had you already remarried?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I didn't. I remarried in 1947. That's why I started giving my son's birthday. It was 47. It was 49 for Dave. But Vance and I were married from 47. And it was a very good marriage except that when I expected Dave, by that time when I paid off the mortgage on the flower shop, I bought a fine new walk-in refrigerator. Or not walk-in, but display refrigerator and display fixtures. Because I had combined... What I had bought was a bunch of broken down nothing. In fact, the people who sold it to me had said, Oh, the flower business, you don't even have to be open for business all the time. You just make sure you have some flowers. I watch the papers. Whenever there's a funeral, get a few flowers in. If you have weddings, they're always booked in advance so you can get some in just for the occasion. Otherwise, oh, there's no point in keeping stock at hand all the time. But see, I had to make something of it or I couldn't afford it. I wasn't... With them, they had other business. There were funeral directors too. And they also owned a lot of rental properties. And they didn't need it for a living. I did. So I tried to make a business out of it. And the one thing that I had learned merchandising of, and also ordering because I did much of the ordering when I was at the hardware store, was the gift line. So I was the first florist in the Inland Empire to incorporate a bag-up gift line with the flower business. I was also the first florist in the Inland Empire to include artificial arrangements. In those days, florists thought that was all going against their business. I said, absolutely not. Sell real flowers with sentiment. Always. But there are some people that are too practical to want real flowers. They want something they can see they've spent the money for this for a long time. And they are not your customers as long as you're selling only flowers. But you gain this extra customer. It wasn't long before I was talking it up in florist meetings and everything else. Now, speaking of learning from scratch, if it's a grocery store, you can sort of check up either openly or on the sly and see how your competitors are doing. See what they're doing. Try to get ideas from what they're doing. When it's a small-town flower shop, there's so often there's no one that you can learn from. Now, there was a competitor shop here. However, the person who was in it was a beautiful designer. She could make the most exotic things you ever saw. The one I bought from was. But Marian was something special in designing. But she had absolutely not the slightest concept in the world about money or what to do with it. She owed everybody in the country. I remember the first year I was in the shop was when the income tax department passed this ruling that merchants should make an estimate of what their income for next year would be. Well, how should I know an estimate? I just bought this. I had no idea what I would be doing for the year. And I talked to Marian about it, who had been one of my friends through the hardware business before. I talked to her about it, and I said, How in the world should I make an estimate about this? She said, Oh, Hazel, forget it. She said, I put my money in the cigar box under the counter. If I need it for something, I take it out of there. There isn't any left. She said, By the time I pay bills and stuff, what I can pay, well, there's never anything left. There's nothing to worry about. You don't even have to file income tax. Well, me, I was so proud of having an income, or thinking I had one, that I wanted to be right with the government as well as the rest of the world. But the gift I incorporated with it, and then later the other, a matchmaker, let me go up, what I was talking about, was when I expected Dave, my first thought was to sell the shop, because I very definitely believe that if the mother has the ability to be anything like a good mother at all, that the children need the association. Now, that doesn't mean that I'm against all mothers working out. There are some mothers who are not half as qualified to be a mother to their children as perhaps someone who is running an accredited nursery. Because all women aren't born mothers, regardless of their physiological aspects. But I had a deep feeling about taking care of a child. So I wanted to sell the flower shop. My husband had a very good shop at the Bunker Hill, it was a cabinet maker in the carpentry shop there. And I knew we could live very well on that, and besides if I sold the shop there'd be a certain income from that. And he says, oh, don't do that. He said, I've always wished that I had a business of my own, and I've been around enough to think that I'd like running a flower shop. You keep it and I'll put it in the bunker and come in it with you, and you can stay home and take care of the baby, and during rushes I'll probably give a hand, but I know I can do it all right. Well, there again, we had a good marriage. But he did not have business savvy, and did not have the sticktuitiveness enough to really see the constant... He'd been used to working for a boss all his life, a boss that had regular hours and would lay out the routine work. And he wasn't... When he worked for a boss, or when the pressure was really on, he wasn't a lazy man. But, oh man, he sure did escape when there was just the seemingly idle time, when the phone wasn't ringing steady or the crowd wasn't in. He couldn't see doing the books or doing this or doing that, the things that needed doing. And also he did not have a good concept, at least at first when it was needed so badly, of the makeup work. He'd seen it, it looked so easy when I did it. But he didn't have... There again, he didn't have the stamina to follow through, to finish things up nicely, and I was an artist in my way. So the result was that I was working day and night, right? Now they tell you that babies don't come more than a couple of weeks overdue. Well, in the first place, my pregnancy was such that I didn't think of it as being pregnancy. I'd been told ten years before that I could not have another child because my uterus was out of place. So I didn't think of this as being a pregnancy. I was 39 years old, and I thought possibly I was having an early change, menopause, because of the fact that my uterus was out of place. So it didn't even occur to me it was a pregnancy. And it went on, and finally there were other signs that... Even then I didn't think of this being pregnancy. I thought perhaps there was tumor or something that was creating a swelling of the breast and a few other palpitations, so I couldn't run up the hill as fast as I used to, and, you know, things like that. So I went to the doctor about it, and it took him about five minutes to tell me I was pregnant. I should have known better. And I told him that he himself had told me many years before that I could not be pregnant. He said, well, physically you can't, but you are. So there it was. Well, it was amazing to me, but not too awfully dismaying. But he said that he could... Now, my dates didn't mean much because, really, I'd gone four or five months without any menstrual period. So my dates didn't mean that much. And he suggested that he just keep examining me, that he could determine. He didn't think I was three months along yet, but he could determine when I was three months along and set the date, project the date from that time, which he did. That was fine. The date was to be April 28th. I forget what time of the year Easter was that year, but it was in April sometime or another. Easter rush at the flower shop is an awful deal. And then right after Easter, there's no rest between Easter and Mother's Day, which is the second Sunday in April. So shortly before Mother's Day, I went into the hospital to have... to have... what do they call the induction shots to see if they couldn't speed up delivery of this child I was carrying and get it over with for Mother's Day. But nothing happened. So I left the hospital again, went back, worked through Mother's Day. My feet were so swollen, they were clear out over the tops of my shoes. And because when I say work, I mean 18, 20 hours a day on my feet. And this went on until after Mother's Day. Immediately after Mother's Day, you get right into the graduation of all the schools and all the corsages and all the hubbub about that, and then right into Decoration Day with all the grave decorations. And in those days, they were very extensive, and there's no letup. So after Mother's Day, we went in for induction shots again. Still nothing happened. And lived through the graduations and the weddings and the Decoration Day work. By that time, I thought, well, from here on out, it gets easier. The child was born on June 9th. I worked all that day. I had a tremendous golden wedding that I was getting flower orders from all over the country for. And they were good friends, both my husband and I. And we were going to the reception. And when I got home, I was going to clean up and get ready to go up to the reception at about 7.30 that night. The reception was at 8. I told my husband to go ahead and change first. I was going to lie down on the diving board a little bit. And by the time he got changed, he said, well, you better get with him. And I said, no, I think I'll just stay here. I said, you go without me. He argued a little bit because he was just used to my going every place with him. We did everything together all through the years. But I said, no, I just couldn't do it. For once, my back ached, my feet were just showing up something terrible, and I just didn't feel like it. So I stayed there, and before he came home, I knew the baby was on its way. And then I kept in the hospital four days then. I was in the hospital four days. When my husband came to pick me up, and the evening was the fourth day, he says, God, you're going to have to come up to the shop and help me get things going up there. I've got a great big funeral for tomorrow, and I don't even know where to start. I haven't even started any of the work yet. And there again, he couldn't organize his mind to do this or do that. He would work like the Dickens when I'd lay out the work for him, but he couldn't organize it. And so I brought the baby home, put him in a bassinet, and fixed a sandwich here for each of us, and went up to the shop, and I worked that night at the work table. I think the baby was a work-aged baby. You had, what time did you say you had to leave?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I've got to leave here at least by 1130, so we have about five more minutes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the flower shop supported us all the years of our marriage anyway. My youngest son had things a lot better than my older boys did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you happy in your second marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Very happy. Very happy. There was a lot of work, but work isn't bad if it's congenial. And in fact, it wasn't work that I talked about in the earlier days. It was the attention, all of his attention. But, you know, Vance was a... He wasn't, he couldn't really operate a business, but he was a congenial sort, he was a very gentle soul, and we shared so much. I never look outside, seeing the rustle of leaves out there, or the shadows on them, that I don't hear Vance saying, hey, hon, come here. See how funny the color is out there, how different that one branch is or something, you know. And he was a very quiet man. But I don't feel bad about his dying, considering that the hardening of the arteries had been taking its toll even the last four or five years we were in the shop, and it was getting progressively worse. And then, not too long after I got rid of the shop, his mind was going more and more blank, until he knew absolutely nothing. All bodily functions were just an accident. I mean, there was no way of explaining anything to him or making him understand any sign of his thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was he much older than you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Eight years. Which, age, you know, is a funny thing. I'll be 66 in December, but I know I'm far more active, both mentally and physically, than some of the people I know down at the rest home in their 50s are far more decrepit than I am. This was the thing that really bugged me when I finally had to put Vance in the rest home after he'd had a stroke or two, so he was paralyzed too, and I couldn't even maneuver him around. And I'd been on guard with him, I would say, for 24 hours a day, so long. But anyway, by the time I put him in there, he didn't know me at all. However, when I go down there to be with him, I knew I would save practically everyone in the rest home from prior acquaintanceship as customers in the shop and so forth. And it was amazing to me how many, many of them were people that I thought of as young people. Some of them no older than my older son. And age is such a weird thing. Now this Mrs. Benning that I spoke to you of, 86 years old, and it's absolutely fantastic how alert she is. I think she may have some difficulty with her legs. She wheels around in the wheelchair much of the time in there, which is quite comfortable now. And she says herself that she has some trouble with her eyes. However, I don't think she's completely blind. But 86.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I need a little more information. Your husband's name was Vance Corveille.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was his birth in place of the date of year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1901. It's the day after. Let's see, November 31st, I guess. Which is Halloween?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: October 31st.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, October 31st. Well, his October 30th then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Phoenix, B.C., which is an extinct town now. His parents have traveled a lot too. However, they were in this. They lived in Murray toward the last of the Gold Rush days in Murray. They lived in Mordner during the earlier boom up there. They lived in Berk, and that was a roaring mining town. But they traveled around a lot too, although all of Vance's schooling was right in this area. He wasn't – he may have gone to Murray School for a year. I don't know if so. It was his first year or so. And he went to school in Calgary, Alberta for a couple of years, but the rest of the schooling was all either in Mordner or Kellogg.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what year were you married then?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Here in Kellogg?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, yes, yes. Sorry to say Wallace because we had a problem getting me over there to get the license signed, but we were married in Kellogg by Reverend Trefft from the United Church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what year did he die then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Vance? A year ago, Thanksgiving.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, it wasn't very long ago. No. 74?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, let's see, 74 was last Thanksgiving. Oh, yeah. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, let me see if there's any other last question I want to ask you. What do you do with your leisure time now? You know, what's your favorite thing to do when you can? I guess most of your time could be considered leisure, even though I'm sure you do it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's all considered my own time now. But as for what's my favorite, I wouldn't know. I, last winter I enrolled in an art class because all my life I wanted to do some oil painting. That's one that I made, and I have another one on the wall back over, you can't see it very well there. But this one over here was the second one that I painted, and the one over there is the third. This little one over here, incidentally, is one that's very big. I have a young son of mine, made in seventh grade. He took one semester of art.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, my God.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So, but then, you see over there is one that's made of dried flowers. The flowers are milkweed pods and rose hips, snorting grape. Every so often I have someone ask me to make one of those for pay. Oh. And I've done quite a few of those.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you learn that through your floral shop there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I created that type of work. As far as the, I have, I received a lot of recognition in the floral industry. Now I learn by myself the hard way. There weren't even books on designing a man for those days. But I studied pictures, I studied painting, I studied everything. By studied, I mean on my own, you know. In reading the papers, watching social pictures in the paper, I looked at bridal bouquets in the Spokesman Society section. And I studied every available thing as to how to put flowers together to come out with pleasing designs at a profit. But as time went on, the Inland Empire florists had a little design competition just to see how it would go. And I don't know, I suppose we were about 30 at the meeting, and I brought a little design too, really quite routine. Well, mine was unanimously voted the best one there. Later on, the Northwest Florist Association had a design competition at their Northwest Convention, which includes seven states and two provinces. And there was absolutely no way that anyone could tell who had made anything because you were given a number, and you put a number on the thing, and you had the other number, which was put into a closed box, you see, that had your name on that one. But there was no way they could discover who had made any of the things unless they went around and say, hey, I made that one, vote for it. And then they balloted. These were all professional florists, retail florists that knew designing. And little old Hazel from the little old small town of Kellogg got first prize.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, isn't that nice?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a little trophy someplace or another collecting dust or mildew for that. But in the Florist Association also, I joined the FTD, the Florist Telegraph Delivery Service. It was called then now Florist Transworld. But I joined it as soon as I qualified for it. And I was the first woman ever elected chairman of the Inland Empire unit of the FTD. And then I was the first woman elected as a district representative to national meetings from the Inland Empire. Now the Inland Empire includes everything from Grangeville, Idaho, up to Kamloops, Kimberly, Trail, B.C., Nelson, all of those towns up there in Onup, and over to Kalispell, Montana, and up through the Okanagan in Washington. It's a large area. Incidentally, when I was the district representative to national, the continent was divided into 91 districts. Only 10 districts were represented by women. Ten out of 91. So it was a man's world, even though small-timers think of flowers as being a woman's job. It was really a man's world from the business end of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Okay. I want to ask you one last question real quickly here. What are some of the reasons or the factors that have made you stay in this small town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because you just happened to get dumped there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just happened to be here and established your business.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There were always responsibilities here. There was a series of strikes in this town following World War II. You see, wages and prices were frozen during the World War II.
